lessons.title: Brooder Setup: Temperature, Bedding, and Space for Guinea Keets and Quail Chicks
lessons.body:
A brooder is a warm, safe box for chicks. For guinea keets and quail chicks, you need a brooder that keeps them at 35Â°C (95Â°F) in the first week. Use a 100-watt bulb for every 30 chicks. Hang the bulb 45 cm above the floor. Raise it by 7 cm each week to lower the temperature by about 3Â°C. By week 4, they need 24Â°C. Watch the chicks: if they huddle under the bulb, they are cold; if they spread to corners, they are too hot. They should be evenly spread.

For bedding, use wood shavings, not sawdust (chicks eat it and get sick). Rice husks or chopped straw also work. Spread 5 cm deep. Never use newspaperâit causes leg problems. Clean bedding every 2 days. Wet bedding grows mold and bacteria.

Space is critical. Guinea keets need 0.5 square feet per bird in week 1, increasing to 1 square foot by week 4. Quail chicks are smaller: 0.25 square feet per bird in week 1, up to 0.5 square feet by week 4. Overcrowding leads to pecking and disease. Use a cardboard box or wooden crate. For 50 keets, start with a box 1m x 1m. Cover the top with wire mesh to keep out rats and snakes. Place the brooder in a quiet, dry place away from drafts.

Before chicks arrive, warm the brooder for 2 hours. Dip each chick's beak in water with vitamins (see Lesson 2). Then put them under the bulb. Check them every 2 hours for the first day. Adjust the bulb height as needed.

lessons.title: Feeding Chicks: Starter Feed and Water with Vitamins
lessons.body:
Chicks need starter feed with 24% protein for guinea keets and 28% for quail chicks. Buy commercial chick starter mash or crumbles. If unavailable, mix your own: 50% maize meal, 20% soybean meal, 15% fish meal, 10% groundnut cake, 5% minerals and vitamins. Grind finelyâchicks cannot swallow large pieces. Feed them every 3 hours for the first week, then 4 times a day. Use a shallow tray or egg carton as a feeder. Clean leftover feed daily to prevent mold.

Water is more important than feed. Chicks can die from dehydration in 6 hours. Use a shallow dish with clean water. Add vitamins and electrolytes for the first 3 days. You can buy chick vitamin drops at agrovet shops. Mix 1 teaspoon per liter of water. Also add 1 tablespoon of glucose (or honey) per liter for energy. Change water 3 times a day. Never let water sitâchicks will poop in it.

For the first 2 days, dip each chick's beak into the water. They learn fast. Use a waterer with a narrow lip to prevent drowning. For quail chicks, put marbles or small stones in the water dish so they don't get soaked.

From week 2, you can add finely chopped green vegetables like kale or amaranth. This gives vitamins and reduces feed costs. But do not exceed 10% of their diet. Always provide grit (small stones) for digestion. A handful of sand in the feed works. By week 4, switch to grower feed with 20% protein. Keep feed and water available at all timesâchicks eat little but often.

lessons.title: Common Chick Diseases and Simple Treatments
lessons.body:
The most common killer is coccidiosis. Signs: bloody droppings, ruffled feathers, chicks standing hunched. Treat with amprolium (e.g., Amprol) in water for 5 days. Prevent by keeping bedding dry and clean. Another killer is Newcastle diseaseâsigns: gasping, twisted neck, green diarrhea. There is no cure; vaccinate (see Lesson 4).

Pullorum disease (white diarrhea) hits chicks under 3 weeks. Signs: white pasty vent, weakness. Treat with antibiotics like oxytetracycline in water for 5 days. Isolate sick chicks immediately. Always wash hands after handling sick birds.

Fowl pox shows as scabs on head and legs. Treat by applying iodine to scabs. Vaccinate at 6 weeks if common in your area. Aspergillosis (brooder pneumonia) comes from moldy bedding. Signs: gasping, no rales. Remove wet bedding, improve ventilation. No cureâprevention is key.

Simple treatments you can do: For diarrhea, give 1 tablespoon of apple cider vinegar per liter of water for 3 days. For respiratory distress, add 1 crushed garlic clove per liter of water. For wounds, clean with warm salt water and apply honey. Keep a sick pen away from healthy chicks. Use a separate waterer and feeder.

Always check with a local vet or extension officer before using any drug. Withdraw antibiotics 5 days before selling eggs or meat. Record all treatments in a notebook. Healthy chicks are active, bright-eyed, and eat well. If you see 3 or more sick chicks, act fastâdisease spreads in hours.

lessons.title: Vaccination Schedule for Guinea Fowl and Quail in Africa
lessons.body:
Vaccines are cheap; dead chicks are expensive. For guinea fowl, start at day 1: Marek's disease vaccine (injected at hatchery). If you hatch at home, skip Marek'sâit's not practical. At day 7: Newcastle disease (ND) vaccine via eye drop or drinking water. Repeat at day 21 and day 42. At day 14: Gumboro (IBD) vaccine in drinking water. Repeat at day 28.

For quail, vaccination is less common but recommended in disease-prone areas. At day 7: Newcastle disease vaccine (eye drop). Repeat every 3 months. Quail are more resistant to some diseases, but ND can wipe a flock. Also vaccinate against fowl pox at 6 weeks if you see cases nearby.

How to vaccinate via drinking water: Withdraw water for 2 hours. Mix vaccine in clean water (no chlorine) with 2 grams of skim milk powder per liter to protect the virus. Give enough for 1 hour of drinking. Use plastic drinkers, not metal. For eye drop: put one drop in one eye, hold chick until it blinks. For injection: use a 1 ml syringe under the skin of the neck.

Store vaccines in a flask with ice. Never freeze. Use within 2 hours of mixing. Buy from a reputable agrovet. In Africa, ND is the biggest killer. Many countries have government vaccination programsâask your local veterinary office. Keep a vaccination record: date, vaccine name, batch number. If you sell chicks, buyers will pay more for vaccinated birds.

lessons.title: Gradual Introduction to Outdoor Pens
lessons.body:
Chicks cannot go outside until they are fully feathered and the weather is warm. For guinea keets, wait until 4-5 weeks. For quail, 3-4 weeks. Start with short periods: 30 minutes on day 1, then add 30 minutes each day. Choose a warm, sunny day with no wind. The outdoor temperature should be at least 24Â°C.

Build a simple outdoor pen: a wooden frame covered with wire mesh on all sides, including the top. The bottom should be wire mesh or concrete to stop digging predators. Size: 1 square meter for 20 keets or 40 quail. Put the pen on grass or dirt, but move it daily to fresh ground to avoid disease build-up. Provide shadeâa piece of corrugated iron or palm fronds. Always provide water and feed inside the pen.

Never leave chicks outside unattended. Hawks, snakes, cats, and even rats will kill them. Stay with them or use a secure covered pen. At night, bring them back to the brooder. After 1 week of daily outdoor time, they can stay outside during the day if the pen is predator-proof. By 6 weeks for keets and 5 weeks for quail, they can live outside permanently if the weather is warm. But provide a shelter at night.

Transition slowly: if chicks huddle or shiver, bring them in. If they pant and spread wings, they are too hotâprovide more shade. After 2 weeks of successful outdoor days, you can leave them out overnight in a secure house. This gradual method prevents stress and disease.

lessons.title: Sexing Chicks: Telling Males from Females Early
lessons.body:
Sexing chicks early saves feed and space. For guinea fowl, you cannot sex day-old keets by looking. But at 4-6 weeks, males start to make a one-syllable call 'check' while females make a two-syllable 'buck-wheat'. At 8 weeks, the helmet (casque) on the male's head is larger and more upright. The male's wattles are larger and hang lower. Also, males have a slightly bigger body and coarser feathers. For accurate sexing, wait until 10-12 weeks and check the vent: males have a small bump (papilla) inside the vent, females do not.

For quail, sexing is easier. At 3-4 weeks, males have a reddish-brown breast with dark spots, while females have a lighter, speckled breast. Males also have a larger, more rounded head and a distinct crow. In some breeds like Japanese quail, males have a cloacal gland (a small bump above the vent) that produces a white foam when pressed. Females lack this. You can also look at the feathers: male quail have longer, pointed feathers on the back and neck.

If you are unsure, separate suspected males into a different pen. Watch for mounting behaviorâmales mount females. Also, males fight more. For breeding, keep 1 male to 4 females for guinea fowl and 1 male to 3 females for quail. Too many males cause stress and injury.

A simple trick: hold the chick upside down gently. Males often curl their tail up, females keep it down. But this is not 100% reliable. The best method is vent sexing by an experienced person. If you plan to sell breeding stock, learn vent sexing from a vet or extension officer. Practice on older birds first.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature for guinea keets in the first week?
quiz.explanation: Guinea keets need 35Â°C in the first week, then reduce gradually.

quiz.q: Which bedding material is safe for chicks?
quiz.explanation: Wood shavings are safe; newspaper causes leg problems and sawdust can be eaten.

quiz.q: How much space does a guinea keet need in week 1?
quiz.explanation: Guinea keets need 0.5 square feet per bird in week 1.

quiz.q: What should you do if chicks huddle under the heat bulb?
quiz.explanation: Huddling means they are cold; lower the bulb or increase wattage.

quiz.q: What protein level do quail chicks need in starter feed?
quiz.explanation: Quail chicks need 28% protein starter feed.

quiz.q: How often should you change chick water?
quiz.explanation: Change water at least three times a day to keep it clean.

quiz.q: What can you add to water for the first 3 days to give energy?
quiz.explanation: Glucose or honey provides quick energy to weak chicks.

quiz.q: What is a sign of coccidiosis in chicks?
quiz.explanation: Bloody droppings are a classic sign of coccidiosis.

quiz.q: Which disease has no cure and must be prevented by vaccination?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle disease has no cure; vaccination is the only protection.

quiz.q: What is a simple treatment for diarrhea in chicks?
options: A) Apple cider vinegar in water
quiz.explanation: Apple cider vinegar (1 tbsp per liter) can help with mild diarrhea.

quiz.q: When should guinea fowl receive Newcastle disease vaccine?
quiz.explanation: First ND vaccine is given at day 7, then repeated.

quiz.q: How should vaccines be stored?
options: B) In a flask with ice
quiz.explanation: Vaccines must be kept cool in a flask with ice, never frozen.

quiz.q: What can you add to drinking water to protect the vaccine virus?
quiz.explanation: Skim milk powder (2g per liter) neutralizes chlorine and protects the virus.

quiz.q: At what age can guinea keets go outside for short periods?
quiz.explanation: Guinea keets can start short outdoor periods at 4-5 weeks when fully feathered.

quiz.q: What is a key feature of a good outdoor pen?
options: B) Wire mesh on all sides including top
quiz.explanation: Wire mesh on all sides and top prevents predators from entering.

quiz.q: How often should you move a movable outdoor pen?
quiz.explanation: Move daily to fresh ground to avoid disease build-up.

quiz.q: What is a sign that chicks are too hot outside?
quiz.explanation: Panting and spreading wings indicate overheating.

quiz.q: How can you tell male guinea fowl from females at 4-6 weeks?
options: B) By call: males one-syllable, females two-syllable
quiz.explanation: Males make a one-syllable 'check' call, females a two-syllable 'buck-wheat'.

quiz.q: What is a reliable way to sex quail at 3-4 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Males have reddish-brown breast feathers; females are lighter and speckled.

quiz.q: What is the cloacal gland in male quail used for?
quiz.explanation: The cloacal gland produces a white foam used in mating.

quiz.q: What is the recommended male to female ratio for guinea fowl breeding?
quiz.explanation: One male to four females prevents fighting and stress.

quiz.q: What should you do before putting chicks in the brooder?
options: B) Warm the brooder for 2 hours
quiz.explanation: Pre-warming the brooder ensures chicks are not chilled.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a healthy chick?
quiz.explanation: Healthy chicks are active with bright eyes and good appetite.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do when you receive day-old chicks?
options: B) Dip their beaks in water
quiz.explanation: Dipping beaks in water teaches them to drink and prevents dehydration.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of brooder pneumonia?
quiz.explanation: Aspergillosis (brooder pneumonia) comes from moldy bedding.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is given at day 14 for guinea fowl?
quiz.explanation: Gumboro (IBD) vaccine is given at day 14 and repeated at day 28.

quiz.q: How long should you withdraw water before giving a vaccine in drinking water?
quiz.explanation: Withdraw water for 2 hours so chicks drink the vaccine quickly.

quiz.q: What is the best method for accurate sexing of guinea fowl?
options: B) Vent sexing by experienced person
quiz.explanation: Vent sexing is the most reliable method for guinea fowl.

quiz.q: At what age can quail chicks live outside permanently?
quiz.explanation: Quail can live outside permanently at 5-6 weeks if warm and secure.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see 3 or more sick chicks?
quiz.explanation: Act fast to isolate and treat sick chicks to prevent spread.
